title: Dominant eye, sight alignment and sight picture
subtitle: Aiming the handgun

lines: This episode covers aiming: your dominant eye, sight alignment, and sight picture.
Each person has a dominant eye, and it is important to know which eye should be looking through the sights.

scenes.heading: How your eyes work
bullets: Dominant eye: the direct line of sight
Distance and speed of an object

lines.text: The dominant eye is the eye that looks at the direct line of sight.
The non-dominant eye is the eye that cross references.
It does this to determine the distance of an object from you, or the speed that an object is travelling.

lines: So the dominant eye looks directly at the object.
And the non-dominant eye is responsible for your depth perception, telling your brain the distance of the object.

scenes.heading: How your eyes work
scenes.caption: How Your Eyes Work, left half of the book's diagram
lines: In the book's diagram, the solid line is the dominant eye, looking directly at the object.
The dashed lines show the non-dominant eye cross-referencing, which tells your brain the distance of the object.

scenes.heading: Finding your dominant eye: step 1
scenes.caption: Step 1: hands about 30 centimetres apart
lines: Here's how the book has you determine your dominant eye.
Step one: extend your arms, with your hands about 30 centimetres apart.
Look at an object about 10 feet away, with both eyes open.

scenes.heading: Finding your dominant eye: step 2
scenes.caption: Step 2: bring your hands closer together
lines: Step two: slowly bring your hands closer together, without losing sight of the object you are looking at.

scenes.heading: Finding your dominant eye: step 3
scenes.caption: Step 3: a small aperture, about the size of your eye socket
lines: Step three: close your hands together, leaving a small aperture about the size of your eye socket.
Look through the aperture, with both eyes open, while maintaining sight of the object.

scenes.heading: Finding your dominant eye: step 4
scenes.caption: Step 4: draw your hands back towards your face
lines: Step four: draw your hands back towards your face, without losing sight of the object.
You will automatically draw your hands towards your dominant eye.
It may be necessary to repeat this exercise 3 or 4 times to be sure.

scenes.definition: Correctly aligning the sights without any reference to the target.
lines: Now, sight alignment.
Sight alignment refers to correctly aligning the sights without any reference to the target.

lines.text: On the pistol, this is the front sight.
And this is the rear sight.

scenes.heading: Equal height, equal spacing
scenes.caption: Front sight and rear sight, correctly aligned on the right
lines: The top of the front sight must be level with the top of the rear sight.
And there should be equal amounts of light on either side of the front sight.
The book's drawing labels these equal height and equal spacing.

scenes.heading: Focus on the front sight
bullets: The sights are at different distances from the eye
Your eye can focus on one sight at a time

lines.text: Bear in mind that the sights are at different distances from the eye.
And your eye can only focus on one sight at a time.

lines: Look through a window at an object outside, and you are aware of the window frame, though not focusing on it.
The same is applicable with the sights on a firearm.

lines.text: You will look through the rear sight.
And focus on the front sight.

scenes.heading: Aligning the sights
scenes.caption: Steps 1 to 3 of aligning the sights
lines: One: here we can see the top of the slide, showing the front sight and rear sight.
Two: here we begin to align the sights.
Three: correct sight alignment is now achieved.

rule.text: Equal height, equal light and a consistent squeeze of the trigger while maintaining your sight picture.

lines: The book sums it up in one line.
Equal height, equal light, and a consistent squeeze of the trigger while maintaining your sight picture.

scenes.heading: Sight picture
scenes.caption: Sight picture, side view: eye, sights and target in one line
lines: Next, sight picture.
Now that you have aligned the sights, place the aligned sights on the centre of the target.
If this is done correctly, your eye, the rear sight, the front sight and the target will be in one line.

scenes.heading: Where to focus
scenes.caption: Sight picture, rear view: sharp focus on the front sight
lines: The target and the sights are at different distances from your eye.
So it is impossible to focus on all three of these objects at the same time.
Focus on the front sight, leaving your target and your rear sight slightly blurred.

scenes.definition: The slight moving or shaking you notice, because nobody can hold the sights perfectly still on the target.
lines: Nobody is able to hold the sights perfectly still on the target.
You will notice a slight amount of moving or shaking.
This is known as the arc of movement.

scenes.heading: The Perfect Shot
scenes.caption: Sight pictures, from high left to low right
lines: In the centre of this chart is the perfect shot, with the sights correctly aligned.
Around it, the sights are out of alignment.
The dot shows where each shot would strike, from high left to low right.

rule.text: Focus on the front sight and squeeze the trigger slowly and consistently.

lines: The book gives a golden rule of aiming.
Focus on the front sight, and squeeze the trigger slowly and consistently.

scenes.question: What is correct sight alignment?
options: Front sight higher than the rear sight
Tops level, equal light either side
Front sight on the target, rear sight ignored
lines: Your formative exam asks you to draw correct sight alignment.
So, what is correct sight alignment?
reveal: The top of the front sight is level with the top of the rear sight.
And there are equal amounts of light on either side of the front sight.

scenes.question: In the sight picture, what should be in sharp focus?
lines: One more.
In the sight picture, what should be in sharp focus?
reveal: You should focus on the front sight, leaving your target and your rear sight slightly blurred.

points: Eye, rear sight, front sight, target in one line
Nobody holds still: the arc of movement
lines: So, determine your dominant eye, so you know which eye should be looking through the sights.
Align the sights with equal height and equal light.
Put the aligned sights on the centre of the target, so everything is in one line.
Focus on the front sight, and squeeze the trigger slowly and consistently.
And remember, the slight shaking you see is the arc of movement.
